newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo business climate in May remained bad - poll.
newsitem.headline: Yugo business climate in May remained bad - poll.

text.p: Yugoslav firms saw no improvement in the business climate in May, with lack of cash and credits remaining the major obstacles to raising output, the Belgrade-based Economics Institute said on Monday.

"Businessmen maintained the level of optimism from April with regard to the situation in their firms, with 27.6 percent expecting improvement and 11 percent deterioration," Nikola Fabris, an economist with the institute, told reporters.
The institute conducts a monthly poll among 300 industrial and energy sector firms.
Businessmen said the overall situation in their companies was difficult and economic climate unfavourable, with high risk characterising the coming three-month period.
Lack of working capital and credits remained the dominant limit to raising output in May for 42.6 percent of the polled.
Low demand was the main obstacle for 27.4 percent firms and lack of imported raw materials for 22.3 percent.
The use of capacities slid slightly from 57.82 percent in April to 57.52 percent in May.
Inflationary expectations remained high, but dropped slightly on April thanks to longer-term stability of prices, the institute said.
According to official statistics, in May retail prices rose 0.2 percent against April, when they were 0.1 percent up on the previous month.
"The number of firms not planning exports in the next three months is growing, which is worrying in view of the high trade deficit," Fabris said.
In May, 42.6 percent of the polled did not plan exports in the next three months, up from 40.7 percent in April.
Due to high risk, lack of long-term capital and unsettled relations with international financial institutions, firms were pessimistic on investment prospects in the next three months.
Some 24.3 percent saw the possibility of investments from domestic sources, 12.9 percent from abroad, while the rest said they did not expect any fresh capital inflow.
